state.misconception_label: Does not understand that 2n represents an even number

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: Which of these shows part of the proof that the sum of two odd numbers is even? I got \( \begin{array}{l}2 n+(2 m+1) \\ =2(n+m)+1\end{array} \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you have a jar with two different types of candies: one type is represented by even numbers and the other by odd numbers. When you combine two odd numbers (represented by \(2m+1\)), you end up with an even total number of candies. In this case, the even total number of candies is like the even number \(2(n+m)+1\) you have in your equation. Can you see how this concrete example relates to the abstract concept of the sum of two odd numbers being even?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Um, I think I see what you mean with the candies, but I'm confused because you said the total is even, but then you wrote \(2(n+m)+1\) which has a +1 at the end... doesn't that make it odd? Like, I thought even numbers don't have a +1?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you have two jars of candies: one with even numbers of candies and the other with odd numbers. When you combine two odd numbers of candies, you end up with an even total number of candies. The +1 at the end of \(2(n+m)+1\) represents the extra candy you get when you combine two odd numbers, making the total even. Just like how in our example, the total number of candies is even even though there is an extra one.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher provides mathematically incorrect explanations (claiming 2(n+m)+1 is even, contradicting basic definitions), fails to address the student's core confusion about even/odd representation, and the student's final turn shows increased confusion rather than improvement.
score.justification_pass2: While the teacher attempts to use a concrete candy analogy throughout, the analogy is mathematically incoherent (claiming 2(n+m)+1 is even and that +1 makes things even), which undermines the experiential strategy's goal of grounding abstract concepts in clear, accurate real-world situations.
